    Mobius Inversion

    Möbius inversion is an important technique in number theory. For some functions 𝑓(𝑛)f(n), if it is difficult to directly compute their values, but it is easy to compute their multiple sums or divisor sums 𝑔(𝑛)g(n), then Möbius inversion can be used to simplify the computation and obtain the value of 𝑓(𝑛)f(n).

    The Möbius Function

    The Möbius function is defined as

    𝜇(𝑛)=⎧{ {⎨{ {⎩1,𝑛=1,0,𝑛 is divisible by a square >1,(−1)𝑘,𝑛 is the product of 𝑘 distinct primes.μ(n)={1,n=1,0,n is divisible by a square >1,(−1)k,n is the product of k distinct primes.

    Specifically, suppose the positive integer 𝑛n has the prime factorization 𝑛 =∏𝑘𝑖=1𝑝𝑒𝑖𝑖n=∏i=1kpiei, where 𝑝𝑖pi are primes and 𝑒𝑖ei are positive integers. Then the three cases correspond to:

    1. 𝜇(1) =1μ(1)=1;
    2. When there exists 𝑖i such that 𝑒𝑖 >1ei>1, i.e., any prime factor appears more than once, 𝜇(𝑛) =0μ(n)=0;
    3. Otherwise, for all 𝑖i we have 𝑒𝑖 =1ei=1, i.e., every prime factor appears exactly once, then 𝜇(𝑛) =( −1)𝑘μ(n)=(−1)k, where 𝑘k is the number of distinct prime factors.

    Properties

    According to the definition, it is easy to verify that the Möbius function 𝜇(𝑛)μ(n) is a multiplicative function, but not a completely multiplicative function. Beyond this, the most important property is the following identity:

    Property

    For a positive integer 𝑛n, we have

    ∑𝑑∣𝑛𝜇(𝑑)=[𝑛=1]={1,𝑛=1,0,𝑛≠1.∑d∣nμ(d)=[n=1]={1,n=1,0,n≠1.

    Here [ ⋅][⋅] is the Iverson bracket.

    Proof

    Let 𝑛 =∏𝑘𝑖=1𝑝𝑒𝑖𝑖n=∏i=1kpiei, and let 𝑛′ =∏𝑘𝑖=1𝑝𝑖n′=∏i=1kpi. According to the Binomial Theorem, we have

    ∑𝑑∣𝑛𝜇(𝑑)=∑𝑑∣𝑛′𝜇(𝑑)=𝑘∑𝑖=0(𝑘𝑖)(−1)𝑖=(1+(−1))𝑘=[𝑘=0]=[𝑛=1].∑d∣nμ(d)=∑d∣n′μ(d)=∑i=0k(ki)(−1)i=(1+(−1))k=[k=0]=[n=1].

    Using Dirichlet convolution, this expression can be written as 𝜀 =1 ∗𝜇ε=1∗μ. That is, the Möbius function is the Dirichlet inverse of the constant function 11.

    This property has a very common application:

    [𝑖⟂𝑗]=[gcd(𝑖,𝑗)=1]=∑𝑑∣gcd(𝑖,𝑗)𝜇(𝑑)=∑𝑑[𝑑∣𝑖][𝑑∣𝑗]𝜇(𝑑).[i⟂j]=[gcd(i,j)=1]=∑d∣gcd(i,j)μ(d)=∑d[d∣i][d∣j]μ(d).

    This transforms the coprimality condition into a sum involving the Möbius function, facilitating further derivation.

    Computation Methods

    If we need to compute the Möbius function 𝜇(𝑛)μ(n) for a single 𝑛n, we can use its prime factorization. For example, when 𝑛n is not too large, we can compute 𝜇(𝑛)μ(n) in 𝑂(√𝑛)O(n) time.

    Reference Implementation

    int mu(int n) {
  int res = 1;
  for (int i = 2; i * i <= n; ++i) {
    if (n % i == 0) {
      n /= i;
      // Check if square-free.
      if (n % i == 0) return 0;
      res = -res;
    }
  }
  // The remaining factor must be prime.
  if (n > 1) res = -res;
  return res;
}

    def mu(n):
    res = 1
    i = 2
    while i * i <= n:
        if n % i == 0:
            n //= i
            # Check if square-free
            if n % i == 0:
                return 0
            res = -res
        i += 1
    # The remaining factor must be prime
    if n > 1:
        res = -res
    return res

    If we need to precompute 𝜇(𝑛)μ(n) for the first 𝑛n positive integers, we can use the fact that it is a multiplicative function and compute it in 𝑂(𝑛)O(n) time using the linear sieve.

    std::vector<int> get_mu(int n) {
  std::vector<int> mu(n + 1), primes;
  std::vector<bool> not_prime(n + 1);
  primes.reserve(n);
  mu[1] = 1;
  for (int x = 2; x <= n; ++x) {
    if (!not_prime[x]) {
      primes.push_back(x);
      mu[x] = -1;
    }
    for (int p : primes) {
      if (x * p > n) break;
      not_prime[x * p] = true;
      if (x % p == 0) {
        mu[x * p] = 0;
        break;
      } else {
        mu[x * p] = -mu[x];
      }
    }
  }
  return mu;
}

    def get_mu(n):
    mu = [0] * (n + 1)
    primes = []
    not_prime = [False] * (n + 1)

    mu[1] = 1
    for x in range(2, n + 1):
        if not not_prime[x]:
            primes.append(x)
            mu[x] = -1
        for p in primes:
            if x * p > n:
                break
            not_prime[x * p] = True
            if x % p == 0:
                mu[x * p] = 0
                break
            else:
                mu[x * p] = -mu[x]
    return mu

    Möbius Inversion

    The most important application of the Möbius function is Möbius inversion.

    Möbius Inversion

    Let 𝑓(𝑛),𝑔(𝑛)f(n),g(n) be two number-theoretic functions. Then we have

    𝑓(𝑛)=∑𝑑∣𝑛𝑔(𝑑)⟺𝑔(𝑛)=∑𝑑∣𝑛𝜇(𝑛𝑑)𝑓(𝑑).f(n)=∑d∣ng(d)⟺g(n)=∑d∣nμ(nd)f(d).
    Proof One

    Direct verification:

    ∑𝑑∣𝑛𝜇(𝑛𝑑)𝑓(𝑑)=∑𝑑∣𝑛𝜇(𝑛𝑑)∑𝑘∣𝑑𝑔(𝑘)=∑𝑘∣𝑛𝑔(𝑘)∑𝑑[𝑘∣𝑑∣𝑛]𝜇(𝑛𝑑)=∑𝑘∣𝑛𝑔(𝑘)∑𝑑∣𝑛[𝑛𝑑∣𝑛𝑘]𝜇(𝑛𝑑)=∑𝑘∣𝑛𝑔(𝑘)[𝑛𝑘=1]=𝑔(𝑛).∑d∣nμ(nd)f(d)=∑d∣nμ(nd)∑k∣dg(k)=∑k∣ng(k)∑d[k∣d∣n]μ(nd)=∑k∣ng(k)∑d∣n[nd∣nk]μ(nd)=∑k∣ng(k)[nk=1]=g(n).

    The key to the transformation is swapping the order of summation and noting that 𝑘 ∣𝑑 ∣𝑛k∣d∣n is equivalent to 𝑛𝑑 ∣𝑛𝑘nd∣nk. The second-to-last equality corresponds to summing the Möbius function at 𝑛𝑑nd over all divisors 𝑛𝑑nd of 𝑛𝑘nk, which equals [𝑛𝑘=1][nk=1]. This expression is nonzero only at 𝑛 =𝑘n=k, and finally we obtain 𝑔(𝑛)g(n).

    Proof Two

    Using Dirichlet convolution, the proposition is equivalent to

    𝑓=1∗𝑔⟺𝑔=𝜇∗𝑓.f=1∗g⟺g=μ∗f.

    Using 1 ∗𝜇 =𝜀1∗μ=ε, convolving both sides of the left equation with 𝜇μ gives

    𝑓∗𝜇=(1∗𝑔)∗𝜇=(1∗𝜇)∗𝑔=𝜀∗𝑔=𝑔.f∗μ=(1∗g)∗μ=(1∗μ)∗g=ε∗g=g.

    Möbius inversion is a powerful transformation tool for sums involving various divisibility relations of number-theoretic functions.

    Examples

    1. Euler's totient function 𝜑(𝑛)φ(n) satisfies 𝑛 =∑𝑑∣𝑛𝜑(𝑑)n=∑d∣nφ(d), i.e., id =1 ∗𝜑id=1∗φ. Applying inversion gives 𝜑 =𝜇 ∗idφ=μ∗id, i.e.,

      𝜑(𝑛)=∑𝑑∣𝑛𝑑𝜇(𝑛𝑑).φ(n)=∑d∣ndμ(nd).

    2. The divisor function 𝜎𝑘(𝑛) =∑𝑑∣𝑛𝑑𝑘σk(n)=∑d∣ndk, i.e., 𝜎𝑘 =1 ∗id𝑘σk=1∗idk. Applying inversion gives id𝑘 =𝜇 ∗𝜎𝑘idk=μ∗σk, i.e.,

      𝑛𝑘=∑𝑑∣𝑛𝜇(𝑛𝑑)𝜎𝑘(𝑑).nk=∑d∣nμ(nd)σk(d).

    3. The number of distinct prime factors function 𝜔(𝑛) =∑𝑑∣𝑛[𝑑 ∈𝐏]ω(n)=∑d∣n[d∈P], i.e., 𝜔 =1 ∗𝟏𝐏ω=1∗1P, where 𝟏𝐏1P is the indicator function of the prime set 𝐏P. Applying inversion gives 𝟏𝐏 =𝜇 ∗𝜔1P=μ∗ω, i.e.,

      [𝑛∈𝐏]=∑𝑑∣𝑛𝜇(𝑛𝑑)𝜔(𝑑).[n∈P]=∑d∣nμ(nd)ω(d).

    4. Consider the number-theoretic function Λ(𝑛)Λ(n) satisfying log⁡𝑛 =∑𝑑∣𝑛Λ(𝑑)log⁡n=∑d∣nΛ(d). This is the Möbius inversion of the logarithm function, also called the von Mangoldt function:

      Λ(𝑛)=∑𝑑∣𝑛𝜇(𝑛𝑑)log⁡𝑑={log⁡𝑝,𝑛=𝑝𝑒, 𝑝∈𝐏, 𝑒∈𝐍+,0,otherwise.Λ(n)=∑d∣nμ(nd)log⁡d={log⁡p,n=pe, p∈P, e∈N+,0,otherwise.
    Proof of the expression for Λ(𝑛)Λ(n)

    For prime powers 𝑛 =𝑝𝑒 (𝑒 ∈𝐍+)n=pe (e∈N+), we have

    Λ(𝑛)=𝑒∑𝑖=0𝜇(𝑝𝑒−𝑖)log⁡𝑝𝑖=log⁡𝑝𝑒−log⁡𝑝𝑒−1=log⁡𝑝.Λ(n)=∑i=0eμ(pe−i)log⁡pi=log⁡pe−log⁡pe−1=log⁡p.

    For 𝑛 =1n=1, we obviously have Λ(𝑛) =log⁡1 =0Λ(n)=log⁡1=0. For other composite numbers 𝑛n, we have

    Λ(𝑛)=∑𝑑∣𝑛𝜇(𝑑)(log⁡𝑛−log⁡𝑑)=⎛⎜ ⎜⎝∑𝑑∣𝑛𝜇(𝑑)⎞⎟ ⎟⎠log⁡𝑛−∑𝑑∣𝑛𝜇(𝑑)log⁡𝑑.Λ(n)=∑d∣nμ(d)(log⁡n−log⁡d)=(∑d∣nμ(d))log⁡n−∑d∣nμ(d)log⁡d.

    According to the property of the Möbius function, the coefficient of log⁡𝑛log⁡n is [𝑛 =1] =0[n=1]=0. For the latter term, we can further decompose 𝑑d into the product of prime factors. For any prime 𝑝 ∣𝑛p∣n, consider the coefficient of log⁡𝑝log⁡p:

    −∑𝑝∣𝑑∣𝑛𝜇(𝑑)=∑(𝑑/𝑝)∣(𝑛/𝑝)𝜇(𝑑𝑝)=[𝑛𝑝=1]=0.−∑p∣d∣nμ(d)=∑(d/p)∣(n/p)μ(dp)=[np=1]=0.

    Thus, for composite numbers 𝑛n with more than one prime factor, we have Λ(𝑛) =0Λ(n)=0.

    Extended Forms

    In addition to the basic form above, there are some common extended forms of Möbius inversion. First, consider its multiple sum form.

    Extension One

    Let 𝑓(𝑛),𝑔(𝑛)f(n),g(n) be two number-theoretic functions. Then we have

    𝑓(𝑛)=∑𝑛∣𝑑𝑔(𝑑)⟺𝑔(𝑛)=∑𝑛∣𝑑𝜇(𝑑𝑛)𝑓(𝑑).f(n)=∑n∣dg(d)⟺g(n)=∑n∣dμ(dn)f(d).
    Proof

    Direct verification:

    ∑𝑛∣𝑑𝜇(𝑑𝑛)𝑓(𝑑)=∑𝑛∣𝑑𝜇(𝑑𝑛)∑𝑑∣𝑘𝑔(𝑘)=∑𝑛∣𝑘𝑔(𝑘)∑𝑑[𝑛∣𝑑∣𝑘]𝜇(𝑑𝑛)=∑𝑛∣𝑘𝑔(𝑘)∑𝑛∣𝑑[𝑑𝑛∣𝑘𝑛]𝜇(𝑑𝑛)=∑𝑛∣𝑘𝑔(𝑘)[𝑘𝑛=1]=𝑔(𝑛).∑n∣dμ(dn)f(d)=∑n∣dμ(dn)∑d∣kg(k)=∑n∣kg(k)∑d[n∣d∣k]μ(dn)=∑n∣kg(k)∑n∣d[dn∣kn]μ(dn)=∑n∣kg(k)[kn=1]=g(n).

    This is completely symmetric to the derivation of the basic form.

    Next, Möbius inversion is not limited to addition; in fact, it works for any operation in any Abel group. For example, it has the following multiplicative form:

    Extension Two

    Let 𝑓(𝑛),𝑔(𝑛)f(n),g(n) be two number-theoretic functions. Then we have

    𝑓(𝑛)=∏𝑑∣𝑛𝑔(𝑑)⟺𝑔(𝑛)=∏𝑑∣𝑛𝑓(𝑑)𝜇(𝑛/𝑑).f(n)=∏d∣ng(d)⟺g(n)=∏d∣nf(d)μ(n/d).
    Proof

    Direct verification:

    ∏𝑑∣𝑛𝑓(𝑑)𝜇(𝑛/𝑑)=∏𝑑∣𝑛⎛⎜ ⎜⎝∏𝑘∣𝑑𝑔(𝑘)⎞⎟ ⎟⎠𝜇(𝑛/𝑑)=∏𝑘∣𝑛𝑔(𝑘)↑(∑𝑑[𝑘∣𝑑∣𝑛]𝜇(𝑛𝑑))=∏𝑘∣𝑛𝑔(𝑘)↑⎛⎜ ⎜⎝∑𝑑∣𝑛[𝑛𝑑∣𝑛𝑘]𝜇(𝑛𝑑)⎞⎟ ⎟⎠=∏𝑘∣𝑛𝑔(𝑘)↑[𝑛𝑘=1]=𝑔(𝑛).∏d∣nf(d)μ(n/d)=∏d∣n(∏k∣dg(k))μ(n/d)=∏k∣ng(k)↑(∑d[k∣d∣n]μ(nd))=∏k∣ng(k)↑(∑d∣n[nd∣nk]μ(nd))=∏k∣ng(k)↑[nk=1]=g(n).

    Here, 𝑎 ↑𝑏 =𝑎𝑏a↑b=ab is Knuth's up-arrow notation. Comparing with the proof of the basic form, the only difference is that addition is replaced by multiplication, and multiplication is replaced by exponentiation.

    From the perspective of Dirichlet convolution, Möbius inversion only uses the fact that "the Möbius function is the Dirichlet inverse of the constant function". It is easy to imagine that similar inversion relationships hold for general Dirichlet inverses as well.

    Extension Three

    Let 𝑓(𝑛),𝑔(𝑛),𝛼(𝑛)f(n),g(n),α(n) all be number-theoretic functions, and 𝛼−1(𝑛)α−1(n) is the Dirichlet inverse of 𝛼(𝑛)α(n), i.e.,

    [𝑛=1]=∑𝑑∣𝑛𝛼(𝑛𝑑)𝛼−1(𝑑).[n=1]=∑d∣nα(nd)α−1(d).

    Then we have

    𝑓(𝑛)=∑𝑑∣𝑛𝛼(𝑛𝑑)𝑔(𝑑)⟺𝑔(𝑛)=∑𝑑∣𝑛𝛼−1(𝑛𝑑)𝑓(𝑑).f(n)=∑d∣nα(nd)g(d)⟺g(n)=∑d∣nα−1(nd)f(d).
    Proof

    Direct verification:

    ∑𝑑∣𝑛𝛼−1(𝑛𝑑)𝑓(𝑑)=∑𝑑∣𝑛𝛼−1(𝑛𝑑)∑𝑘∣𝑑𝛼(𝑑𝑘)𝑔(𝑘)=∑𝑘∣𝑛𝑔(𝑘)∑𝑑[𝑘∣𝑑∣𝑛]𝛼(𝑑𝑘)𝛼−1(𝑛𝑑)=∑𝑘∣𝑛𝑔(𝑘)∑𝑑∣𝑛[𝑛𝑑∣𝑛𝑘]𝛼(𝑑𝑘)𝛼−1(𝑛/𝑘𝑑/𝑘)=∑𝑘∣𝑛𝑔(𝑘)[𝑛𝑘=1]=𝑔(𝑛).∑d∣nα−1(nd)f(d)=∑d∣nα−1(nd)∑k∣dα(dk)g(k)=∑k∣ng(k)∑d[k∣d∣n]α(dk)α−1(nd)=∑k∣ng(k)∑d∣n[nd∣nk]α(dk)α−1(n/kd/k)=∑k∣ng(k)[nk=1]=g(n).

    Compared with the proof of the basic form, we only need to replace the second-to-last equality with the definition of the Dirichlet inverse.

    Corollary

    Let 𝑓(𝑛),𝑔(𝑛)f(n),g(n) be number-theoretic functions, and 𝑡(𝑛)t(n) is a completely multiplicative function. Then we have

    𝑓(𝑛)=∑𝑑∣𝑛𝑡(𝑛𝑑)𝑔(𝑑)⟺𝑔(𝑛)=∑𝑑∣𝑛𝜇(𝑛𝑑)𝑡(𝑛𝑑)𝑓(𝑑).f(n)=∑d∣nt(nd)g(d)⟺g(n)=∑d∣nμ(nd)t(nd)f(d).
    Proof

    According to the properties of Dirichlet convolution, for a completely multiplicative function 𝑡(𝑛)t(n), its Dirichlet inverse is 𝜇(𝑛)𝑡(𝑛)μ(n)t(n).

    Finally, Möbius inversion can also be extended to complex-valued functions on [1, +∞)[1,+∞), not limited to number-theoretic functions. The basic form of Möbius inversion can be seen as a special case of complex-valued functions that take zero at all non-integer points.

    Extension Four

    Let 𝐹(𝑥)F(x) and 𝐺(𝑥)G(x) both be complex-valued functions on [1, +∞)[1,+∞). Then we have

    𝐹(𝑥)=⌊𝑥⌋∑𝑛=1𝐺(𝑥𝑛)⟺𝐺(𝑥)=⌊𝑥⌋∑𝑛=1𝜇(𝑛)𝐹(𝑥𝑛).F(x)=∑n=1⌊x⌋G(xn)⟺G(x)=∑n=1⌊x⌋μ(n)F(xn).
    Proof

    We can extend the definitions of 𝐹F and 𝐺G. Let 𝐹(𝑥) =𝐺(𝑥) =0F(x)=G(x)=0 when 𝑥 <1x<1. Then the proposition is equivalent to:

    𝐹(𝑥)=∑𝑛𝐺(𝑥𝑛)⟺𝐺(𝑥)=∑𝑛𝜇(𝑛)𝐹(𝑥𝑛).F(x)=∑nG(xn)⟺G(x)=∑nμ(n)F(xn).

    These sums are over 𝑛 ∈𝐍+n∈N+.

    Direct verification:

    ∑𝑛𝜇(𝑛)𝐹(𝑥𝑛)=∑𝑛𝜇(𝑛)∑𝑑𝐺(𝑥/𝑛𝑑)=∑𝑘𝐺(𝑥𝑘)∑𝑛∣𝑘𝜇(𝑛)=∑𝑘𝐺(𝑥𝑘)[𝑘=1]=𝐺(𝑥).∑nμ(n)F(xn)=∑nμ(n)∑dG(x/nd)=∑kG(xk)∑n∣kμ(n)=∑kG(xk)[k=1]=G(x).

    Here, to get the second equality, we let 𝑘 =𝑛𝑑k=nd.

    Corollary

    Let 𝑓(𝑛),𝑔(𝑛)f(n),g(n) be number-theoretic functions. Then we have

    𝑓(𝑛)=𝑛∑𝑘=1𝑔(⌊𝑛𝑘⌋)⟺𝑔(𝑛)=𝑛∑𝑘=1𝜇(𝑘)𝑓(⌊𝑛𝑘⌋).f(n)=∑k=1ng(⌊nk⌋)⟺g(n)=∑k=1nμ(k)f(⌊nk⌋).
    Proof

    We only need to take 𝐹(𝑥) =𝑓(⌊𝑥⌋)F(x)=f(⌊x⌋) and 𝐺(𝑥) =𝑔(⌊𝑥⌋)G(x)=g(⌊x⌋).

    These extended forms can be combined with each other to obtain more complex inversion relationships.

    Dirichlet Prefix Sum

    Prerequisites: Prefix Sums and Differences

    Consider the basic form of Möbius inversion:

    𝑓(𝑛)=∑𝑑∣𝑛𝑔(𝑑)⟺𝑔(𝑛)=∑𝑑∣𝑛𝜇(𝑛𝑑)𝑓(𝑑).f(n)=∑d∣ng(d)⟺g(n)=∑d∣nμ(nd)f(d).

    In the left equation, the value 𝑓(𝑛)f(n) is the sum of 𝑔(𝑛)g(n) at all divisors of 𝑛n. If we understand 𝑎 ∣𝑏a∣b as 𝑎a comes before 𝑏b, then 𝑓(𝑛)f(n) can be understood as a kind of prefix sum of 𝑔(𝑛)g(n) in some sense. Therefore, in domestic competition circles, the process of obtaining {𝑓(𝑘)}𝑛𝑘=1{f(k)}k=1n from {𝑔(𝑘)}𝑛𝑘=1{g(k)}k=1n is also called Dirichlet prefix sum, and the inverse process is called Dirichlet difference. These methods mostly appear when precomputing some number-theoretic function at the first 𝑁N points.

    Next, we discuss the computation of Dirichlet prefix sums. If we treat each prime as a dimension, this is a kind of high-dimensional prefix sum. Recall the dimension-by-dimension prefix sum algorithm: iterate through all dimensions one by one, and accumulate each position's value to its successor in that dimension. For number-theoretic functions, this is equivalent to iterating through all primes in increasing order and accumulating the function value at 𝑛n to 𝑛𝑝np. This traversal order is consistent with the Eratosthenes sieve. Therefore, this algorithm can compute the Dirichlet prefix sum of a sequence of length 𝑛n in 𝑂(𝑛log⁡log⁡𝑛)O(nlog⁡log⁡n) time. Similarly, using dimension-by-dimension differences, we can compute the Dirichlet difference of the sequence in the same time complexity.

    std::vector<int> dirichlet_presum(const std::vector<int>& g) {
  int n = g.size() - 1;
  std::vector<int> f(g);
  std::vector<bool> vis(n + 1);
  for (int x = 2; x <= n; ++x) {
    if (vis[x]) continue;
    for (int y = 1, xy = x; xy <= n; ++y, xy += x) {
      vis[xy] = true;
      f[xy] += f[y];
    }
  }
  return f;
}

    std::vector<int> dirichlet_diff(const std::vector<int>& f) {
  int n = f.size() - 1;
  std::vector<int> g(f);
  std::vector<int> vis(n + 1);
  for (int x = 2; x <= n; ++x) {
    if (vis[x]) continue;
    for (int y = n / x, xy = x * y; y; --y, xy -= x) {
      vis[xy] = true;
      g[xy] -= g[y];
    }
  }
  return g;
}

    This computation method can be extended to the multiple sum form (Extension One), the product form (Extension Two), and using a completely multiplicative function instead of the constant function (the corollary of Extension Three).

    Example Problems

    This section demonstrates the application methods of Möbius inversion and some common transformation techniques through example problems. First, let's get familiar with the basic technique for handling gcd conditions in sums through an example.

    Luogu P2522 [HAOI 2011] Problem b

    𝑇T test cases. For each test case, compute:

    𝑛∑𝑖=𝑥𝑚∑𝑗=𝑦[gcd(𝑖,𝑗)=𝑘].∑i=xn∑j=ym[gcd(i,j)=k].

    Constraints: 1 ≤𝑇,𝑥,𝑦,𝑛,𝑚,𝑘 ≤5 ×1041≤T,x,y,n,m,k≤5×104.

    Solution

    According to the principle of inclusion-exclusion, the original expression can be divided into 44 blocks, and each block has the form

    𝑓(𝑛,𝑚,𝑘)=𝑛∑𝑖=1𝑚∑𝑗=1[gcd(𝑖,𝑗)=𝑘].f(n,m,k)=∑i=1n∑j=1m[gcd(i,j)=k].

    For this type of expression, the following is a standard derivation process: extract the common factor, apply the Möbius function property, and swap the order of summation.

    First, since 𝑖i and 𝑗j can only take multiples of 𝑘k, we can factor this out first—this is equivalent to substituting 𝑖 =𝑘𝑖′i=ki′ and 𝑗 =𝑘𝑗′j=kj′:

    𝑓(𝑛,𝑚,𝑘)=⌊𝑛/𝑘⌋∑𝑖=1⌊𝑚/𝑘⌋∑𝑗=1[gcd(𝑖,𝑗)=1].f(n,m,k)=∑i=1⌊n/k⌋∑j=1⌊m/k⌋[gcd(i,j)=1].

    Then, using the property of the Möbius function:

    [gcd(𝑖,𝑗)=1]=∑𝑑∣gcd(𝑖,𝑗)𝜇(𝑑)=∑𝑑[𝑑∣𝑖][𝑑∣𝑗]𝜇(𝑑).[gcd(i,j)=1]=∑d∣gcd(i,j)μ(d)=∑d[d∣i][d∣j]μ(d).

    Substitute it into the expression and swap the order of summation:

    𝑓(𝑛,𝑚,𝑘)=∑𝑑𝜇(𝑑)(⌊𝑛/𝑘⌋∑𝑖=1[𝑑∣𝑖])(⌊𝑚/𝑘⌋∑𝑗=1[𝑑∣𝑗]).f(n,m,k)=∑dμ(d)(∑i=1⌊n/k⌋[d∣i])(∑j=1⌊m/k⌋[d∣j]).

    The benefit of this transformation is that when 𝑑d is fixed, the terms involving 𝑖i and 𝑗j in the sum are separated and can be summed separately. Next, because

    ⌊𝑛/𝑘⌋∑𝑖=1[𝑑∣𝑖]=⌊⌊𝑛/𝑘⌋𝑑⌋, ⌊𝑚/𝑘⌋∑𝑗=1[𝑑∣𝑗]=⌊⌊𝑚/𝑘⌋𝑑⌋,∑i=1⌊n/k⌋[d∣i]=⌊⌊n/k⌋d⌋, ∑j=1⌊m/k⌋[d∣j]=⌊⌊m/k⌋d⌋,

    we have

    𝑓(𝑛,𝑚,𝑘)=∑𝑑𝜇(𝑑)⌊⌊𝑛/𝑘⌋𝑑⌋⌊⌊𝑚/𝑘⌋𝑑⌋.f(n,m,k)=∑dμ(d)⌊⌊n/k⌋d⌋⌊⌊m/k⌋d⌋.

    After preprocessing 𝜇(𝑑)μ(d) with a linear sieve and its prefix sums, we can solve it using number theoretic blocks. The total time complexity is 𝑂(𝑁 +𝑇√𝑁)O(N+TN), where 𝑁N is the upper bound of 𝑛,𝑚n,m, and 𝑇T is the number of test cases.

    #include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;
constexpr int N = 50000;
int mu[N + 5], p[N + 5];
bool flg[N + 5];

void init() {
  int tot = 0;
  mu[1] = 1;
  for (int i = 2; i <= N; ++i) {
    if (!flg[i]) {
      p[++tot] = i;
      mu[i] = -1;
    }
    for (int j = 1; j <= tot && i * p[j] <= N; ++j) {
      flg[i * p[j]] = true;
      if (i % p[j] == 0) {
        mu[i * p[j]] = 0;
        break;
      }
      mu[i * p[j]] = -mu[i];
    }
  }
  for (int i = 1; i <= N; ++i) mu[i] += mu[i - 1];
}

int solve(int n, int m) {
  int res = 0;
  for (int i = 1, j; i <= min(n, m); i = j + 1) {
    j = min(n / (n / i), m / (m / i));
    res += (mu[j] - mu[i - 1]) * (n / i) * (m / i);  // Substitute into the derived formula
  }
  return res;
}

int main() {
  cin.tie(nullptr)->sync_with_stdio(false);
  int T, a, b, c, d, k;
  init();  // Preprocess the mu array
  cin >> T;
  for (int i = 1; i <= T; i++) {
    cin >> a >> b >> c >> d >> k;
    // By inclusion-exclusion, take the answer count in 1<=x<=b&&1<=y<=d, subtract the counts in
    //   1<=x<=b&&1<=y<=c-1 and 1<=x<=a-1&&1<=y<=d, then add the count in
    //   1<=x<=a-1&&1<=y<=c-1 to get the answer count in a<=x<=b&&c<=y<=d
    // If this step is unclear, drawing the coordinate diagram can help
    cout << solve(b / k, d / k) - solve(b / k, (c - 1) / k) -
                solve((a - 1) / k, d / k) + solve((a - 1) / k, (c - 1) / k)
         << '\n';
  }
  return 0;
}

    The next two example problems demonstrate the method of enumerating common divisors and using the sieve to compute general multiplicative function values.

    SPOJ LCMSUM

    𝑇T test cases. For each test case, compute:

    𝑛∑𝑖=1lcm⁡(𝑖,𝑛).∑i=1nlcm⁡(i,n).

    Constraints: 1 ≤𝑇 ≤3 ×105, 1 ≤𝑛 ≤1061≤T≤3×105, 1≤n≤106.

    Solution One

    The problem provides the least common multiple, but the greatest common divisor is often easier to handle. So first, transform:

    𝑓(𝑛)=𝑛∑𝑖=1lcm⁡(𝑖,𝑛)=𝑛∑𝑖=1𝑖⋅𝑛gcd(𝑖,𝑛).f(n)=∑i=1nlcm⁡(i,n)=∑i=1ni⋅ngcd(i,n).

    Factor out 𝑛n, and enumerate the greatest common divisor 𝑘k:

    𝑓(𝑛)=𝑛∑𝑘∣𝑛𝑛∑𝑖=1𝑖𝑘[gcd(𝑖,𝑛)=𝑘].f(n)=n∑k∣n∑i=1nik[gcd(i,n)=k].

    For the inner sum, this is the most common case involving the greatest common divisor. Following the standard processing:

    𝑓(𝑛)=𝑛∑𝑘∣𝑛𝑛/𝑘∑𝑖=1𝑖[gcd(𝑖,𝑛𝑘)=1]=𝑛∑𝑘∣𝑛𝑛/𝑘∑𝑖=1𝑖∑𝑑𝜇(𝑑)[𝑑∣𝑖][𝑑∣𝑛𝑘]=𝑛∑𝑘∣𝑛∑𝑑𝜇(𝑑)[𝑑∣𝑛𝑘](𝑛/𝑘∑𝑖=1𝑖[𝑑∣𝑖]).f(n)=n∑k∣n∑i=1n/ki[gcd(i,nk)=1]=n∑k∣n∑i=1n/ki∑dμ(d)[d∣i][d∣nk]=n∑k∣n∑dμ(d)[d∣nk](∑i=1n/ki[d∣i]).

    Again, the sum involving 𝑖i is separated from the other parts and can be handled separately. The final sum is actually an arithmetic series sum: (taking 𝑖 =𝑑𝑖′i=di′)

    𝑛/𝑘∑𝑖=1𝑖[𝑑∣𝑖]=𝑑12(𝑛𝑘𝑑+1)𝑛𝑘𝑑=:𝑑𝐺(𝑛𝑘𝑑).∑i=1n/ki[d∣i]=d12(nkd+1)nkd=:dG(nkd).

    From this, we obtain:

    𝑓(𝑛)=𝑛∑𝑘∣𝑛∑𝑑𝜇(𝑑)[𝑑∣𝑛𝑘]𝑑𝐺(𝑛𝑘𝑑).f(n)=n∑k∣n∑dμ(d)[d∣nk]dG(nkd).

    After enumerating common divisors, such double sums are very common. For them, there is also a standard method: set the product as a new variable ℓ =𝑘𝑑ℓ=kd, then swap the order of summation again. Since 𝑑 ∣(𝑛/𝑘)d∣(n/k) is equivalent to 𝑑 ∣ℓ ∣𝑛d∣ℓ∣n, the original expression becomes:

    𝑓(𝑛)=𝑛∑ℓ∣𝑛𝐺(𝑛ℓ)∑𝑑∣ℓ𝜇(𝑑)𝑑.f(n)=n∑ℓ∣nG(nℓ)∑d∣ℓμ(d)d.

    Let 𝐹(ℓ) =∑𝑑∣ℓ𝜇(𝑑)𝑑F(ℓ)=∑d∣ℓμ(d)d, then the original expression has the form:

    𝑓(𝑛)=𝑛∑ℓ∣𝑛𝐺(𝑛ℓ)𝐹(ℓ).f(n)=n∑ℓ∣nG(nℓ)F(ℓ).

    Since 𝜇(𝑑)𝑑μ(d)d is a multiplicative function, its convolution with the constant function 11, 𝐹(𝑛)F(n), is also a multiplicative function. Although the sum in the above expression has the form of Dirichlet convolution, 𝐺(𝑛)G(n) is not a multiplicative function, so the whole sum is not a multiplicative function. However, 𝐺(𝑛)G(n) is a polynomial, so it is actually a linear combination of several completely multiplicative functions. Therefore, we have

    𝑓(𝑛)=12𝑛(∑ℓ(𝑛ℓ)2𝐹(ℓ)+∑ℓ𝑛ℓ𝐹(ℓ)).f(n)=12n(∑ℓ(nℓ)2F(ℓ)+∑ℓnℓF(ℓ)).

    These two terms (excluding the coefficient) are multiplicative functions and can be directly precomputed with a linear sieve (or after computing the inner function with linear sieve, precomputed with Dirichlet prefix sum in 𝑂(𝑁log⁡log⁡𝑁)O(Nlog⁡log⁡N) time). Specifically, let

    𝐻𝑠(𝑛)=∑ℓ(𝑛ℓ)𝑠𝐹(ℓ), 𝑠=1,2.Hs(n)=∑ℓ(nℓ)sF(ℓ), s=1,2.

    To derive their expressions, we only need to determine their values at prime powers. For a prime 𝑝p and positive exponent 𝑒e, we have

    𝐹(𝑝𝑒)=𝜇(1)+𝜇(𝑝)𝑝+𝑒∑𝑗=2𝜇(𝑝𝑗)𝑝𝑗=1−𝑝,𝐻𝑠(𝑝𝑒)=(𝑝𝑒)𝑠𝐹(1)+𝑒∑𝑗=1(𝑝𝑒−𝑗)𝑠𝐹(𝑝𝑗)=𝑝𝑒𝑠+(1−𝑝)1−𝑝𝑒𝑠1−𝑝𝑠, 𝑠=1,2.F(pe)=μ(1)+μ(p)p+∑j=2eμ(pj)pj=1−p,Hs(pe)=(pe)sF(1)+∑j=1e(pe−j)sF(pj)=pes+(1−p)1−pes1−ps, s=1,2.

    In particular, 𝐻1(𝑝𝑒) ≡1H1(pe)≡1 is a constant function, and

    𝐻2(𝑝𝑒)=𝑝2𝑒+(1−𝑝)1−𝑝2𝑒1−𝑝2=𝐻2(𝑝𝑒−1)+𝑝2𝑒−𝑝2𝑒−1.H2(pe)=p2e+(1−p)1−p2e1−p2=H2(pe−1)+p2e−p2e−1.

    This can be easily solved with a linear sieve. After precomputing 𝐻2(𝑛)H2(n) with a linear sieve, a single query can be solved in 𝑂(1)O(1) time using the expression 𝑓(𝑛) =(𝑛/2)(𝐻2(𝑛) +1)f(n)=(n/2)(H2(n)+1). The total time complexity is 𝑂(𝑁 +𝑇)O(N+T), where 𝑁N is the upper bound of 𝑛n, and 𝑇T is the number of test cases.

    In the reference implementation, due to the special nature of this problem's expression, further derivation is done for the linear sieve part, which is not required. Using only the values at prime powers, preprocessing can still be done in 𝑂(𝑁)O(N) time. These derivations are detailed in Solution Two.

    Solution Two

    For this problem, there is a more flexible approach. As can be seen from Solution One,

    𝑓(𝑛)=𝑛∑𝑘∣𝑛𝑛/𝑘∑𝑖=1𝑖[gcd(𝑖,𝑛𝑘)=1]=𝑛∑𝑘∣𝑛𝐹(𝑛𝑘).f(n)=n∑k∣n∑i=1n/ki[gcd(i,nk)=1]=n∑k∣nF(nk).

    If at this step we do not continue with Möbius inversion, but observe that the following sum is actually the sum of integers not exceeding 𝑑 =𝑛/𝑘d=n/k that are coprime to 𝑑d. For 𝑑 >1d>1, since integers coprime to 𝑑d appear in pairs, i.e., 𝑖i and 𝑑 −𝑖d−i must both be coprime to 𝑑d, we have

    𝐹(𝑑)=𝑛′∑𝑖=1𝑖[𝑖⟂𝑑]=𝑑∑𝑖=1(𝑑−𝑖)[𝑖⟂𝑑]=12𝑑𝑑∑𝑖=1[𝑖⟂𝑑]=12𝑑𝜑(𝑑).F(d)=∑i=1n′i[i⟂d]=∑i=1d(d−i)[i⟂d]=12d∑i=1d[i⟂d]=12dφ(d).

    For 𝑑 =1d=1, we have

    𝐹(𝑑)=1=12+12𝑑𝜑(𝑑).F(d)=1=12+12dφ(d).

    Therefore, the original expression can be written as

    𝑓(𝑛)=12𝑛⎛⎜ ⎜⎝∑𝑑∣𝑛𝑑𝜑(𝑑)+1⎞⎟ ⎟⎠.f(n)=12n(∑d∣ndφ(d)+1).

    Since 𝐺(𝑛) =∑𝑑∣𝑛𝑑𝜑(𝑑)G(n)=∑d∣ndφ(d) is the Dirichlet convolution of the multiplicative function 𝑛𝜑(𝑛)nφ(n) and the constant function 11, it is also a multiplicative function and can be precomputed with a linear sieve. For this, we only need to determine its value at prime powers. For a prime 𝑝p and positive exponent 𝑒e, we have

    𝐺(𝑝𝑒)=1+𝑒∑𝑖=1𝑝𝑒(𝑝𝑒−1)=𝐺(𝑝𝑒−1)+𝑝2𝑒−𝑝2𝑒−1.G(pe)=1+∑i=1epe(pe−1)=G(pe−1)+p2e−p2e−1.

    It can be seen that this expression is consistent with the result derived in Solution One. The total time complexity of this method is still 𝑂(𝑁 +𝑇)O(N+T).

    Finally, using the multiplicative function expression of this problem, we can further optimize the linear sieve computation. For a prime 𝑝p, we have

    𝐺(𝑝)=1−𝑝+𝑝2.G(p)=1−p+p2.

    The key for the linear sieve for general 𝑛n is to compute 𝐺(𝑝𝑛)G(pn). This further divides into two cases. When 𝑝 ⟂𝑛p⟂n, since 𝐺G is multiplicative,

    𝐺(𝑝𝑛)=𝐺(𝑝)𝐺(𝑛).G(pn)=G(p)G(n).

    Otherwise, when 𝑝 ∣𝑛p∣n, let 𝑛 =𝑝𝑒𝑚n=pem with 𝑝 ⟂𝑚p⟂m, then

    𝐺(𝑝𝑛)=𝐺(𝑝𝑒+1)𝐺(𝑚)=𝐺(𝑝𝑒)𝐺(𝑚)+(𝑝2𝑒+2−𝑝2𝑒+1)𝐺(𝑚)=𝐺(𝑛)+(𝑝2𝑒+2−𝑝2𝑒+1)𝐺(𝑚).G(pn)=G(pe+1)G(m)=G(pe)G(m)+(p2e+2−p2e+1)G(m)=G(n)+(p2e+2−p2e+1)G(m).

    Direct verification shows that this expression also holds for the case 𝑝 ⟂𝑛p⟂n. Therefore, we have

    𝐺(𝑛)−𝐺(𝑛𝑝)=(𝑝2𝑒−𝑝2𝑒−1)𝐺(𝑚).G(n)−G(np)=(p2e−p2e−1)G(m).

    Substituting into the above gives

    𝐺(𝑝𝑛)=𝐺(𝑛)+𝑝2(𝐺(𝑛)−𝐺(𝑛𝑝)).G(pn)=G(n)+p2(G(n)−G(np)).

    This simplifies the computation in the linear sieve part. Of course, this derivation is not necessary; for multiplicative functions without special properties, we can directly use 𝐺(𝑝𝑛) =𝐺(𝑝𝑒+1)𝐺(𝑚)G(pn)=G(pe+1)G(m) to complete the linear sieve computation.

    #include <iostream>
constexpr int N = 1000000;
int tot, p[N + 5];
long long g[N + 5];
bool flg[N + 5];  // Marker array

void solve() {
  g[1] = 1;
  for (int i = 2; i <= N; ++i) {
    if (!flg[i]) {
      p[++tot] = i;
      g[i] = (long long)1 * i * (i - 1) + 1;
    }
    for (int j = 1; j <= tot && i * p[j] <= N; ++j) {
      flg[i * p[j]] = true;
      if (i % p[j] == 0) {
        g[i * p[j]] =
            g[i] + (g[i] - g[i / p[j]]) * p[j] * p[j];  // Substitute into the derived formula
        break;
      }
      g[i * p[j]] = g[i] * g[p[j]];
    }
  }
}

using std::cin;
using std::cout;

int main() {
  cin.tie(nullptr)->sync_with_stdio(false);
  int T, n;
  solve();  // Preprocess the g array
  cin >> T;
  for (int i = 1; i <= T; ++i) {
    cin >> n;
    cout << (g[n] + 1) * n / 2 << '\n';
  }
  return 0;
}
    BZOJ 2154 [National Team Training] Crash's Number Table

    Compute:

    𝑛∑𝑖=1𝑚∑𝑗=1lcm⁡(𝑖,𝑗)mod20101009.∑i=1n∑j=1mlcm⁡(i,j)mod20101009.

    Constraints: 1 ≤𝑛,𝑚 ≤1071≤n,m≤107.

    Solution

    Ignore the modulus during derivation. Let

    𝑓(𝑛,𝑚)=𝑛∑𝑖=1𝑚∑𝑗=1lcm⁡(𝑖,𝑗).f(n,m)=∑i=1n∑j=1mlcm⁡(i,j).

    Still converting the least common multiple to the greatest common divisor, enumerating common divisors, and applying the standard processing:

    𝑓(𝑛,𝑚)=∑𝑘𝑛∑𝑖=1𝑚∑𝑗=1𝑖𝑗𝑘[gcd(𝑖,𝑗)=𝑘]=∑𝑘⌊𝑛/𝑘⌋∑𝑖=1⌊𝑚/𝑘⌋∑𝑗=1𝑘𝑖𝑗[gcd(𝑖,𝑗)=1]=∑𝑘⌊𝑛/𝑘⌋∑𝑖=1⌊𝑚/𝑘⌋∑𝑗=1𝑘𝑖𝑗∑𝑑𝜇(𝑑)[𝑑∣𝑖][𝑑∣𝑗]=∑𝑘𝑘∑𝑑𝜇(𝑑)(⌊𝑛/𝑘⌋∑𝑖=1𝑖[𝑑∣𝑖])(⌊𝑚/𝑘⌋∑𝑗=1𝑗[𝑑∣𝑗]).f(n,m)=∑k∑i=1n∑j=1mijk[gcd(i,j)=k]=∑k∑i=1⌊n/k⌋∑j=1⌊m/k⌋kij[gcd(i,j)=1]=∑k∑i=1⌊n/k⌋∑j=1⌊m/k⌋kij∑dμ(d)[d∣i][d∣j]=∑kk∑dμ(d)(∑i=1⌊n/k⌋i[d∣i])(∑j=1⌊m/k⌋j[d∣j]).

    Again, the sum separates 𝑖i and 𝑗j. First compute these inner sums, extract the factor (i.e., take 𝑖 =𝑑𝑖′i=di′):

    ⌊𝑛/𝑘⌋∑𝑖=1𝑖[𝑑∣𝑖]=𝑑⌊⌊𝑛/𝑘⌋/𝑑⌋∑𝑖=1𝑖=𝑑𝐺(⌊⌊𝑛/𝑘⌋𝑑⌋)=𝑑𝐺(⌊𝑛𝑘𝑑⌋).∑i=1⌊n/k⌋i[d∣i]=d∑i=1⌊⌊n/k⌋/d⌋i=dG(⌊⌊n/k⌋d⌋)=dG(⌊nkd⌋).

    Here, 𝐺(𝑛) =12𝑛(𝑛 +1)G(n)=12n(n+1) is the arithmetic series sum, and the last equality uses the property of the floor function. Similarly, the other sum can be computed. Substituting back into the earlier expression:

    𝑓(𝑛,𝑚)=∑𝑘𝑘∑𝑑𝜇(𝑑)𝑑2𝐺(⌊𝑛𝑘𝑑⌋)𝐺(⌊𝑚𝑘𝑑⌋).f(n,m)=∑kk∑dμ(d)d2G(⌊nkd⌋)G(⌊mkd⌋).

    Consistent with the previous case, for such expressions enumerating common divisors, we often need to enumerate the product ℓ =𝑘𝑑ℓ=kd and swap the order of summation again:

    𝑓(𝑛,𝑚)=∑ℓ⎛⎜ ⎜⎝∑𝑑∣ℓ𝜇(𝑑)𝑑ℓ⎞⎟ ⎟⎠𝐺(⌊𝑛ℓ⌋)𝐺(⌊𝑚ℓ⌋).f(n,m)=∑ℓ(∑d∣ℓμ(d)dℓ)G(⌊nℓ⌋)G(⌊mℓ⌋).

    Let

    𝐹(ℓ)=∑𝑑∣ℓ𝜇(𝑑)𝑑ℓ.F(ℓ)=∑d∣ℓμ(d)dℓ.

    This is the product of the multiplicative function ℓℓ and the multiplicative function ∑𝑑∣ℓ𝜇(𝑑)𝑑∑d∣ℓμ(d)d, so it is also a multiplicative function. It can be directly precomputed with a linear sieve, and its prefix sums can also be precomputed. Then 𝑓(𝑛,𝑚)f(n,m) can be computed using number theoretic blocks. The total time complexity is 𝑂(min{𝑛,𝑚})O(min{n,m}).

    #include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int main() {
  constexpr int M = 20101009;
  int n, m;
  std::cin >> n >> m;
  if (n > m) std::swap(n, m);
  std::vector<int> f(n + 1), vis(n + 1), prime;
  prime.reserve(n);
  f[1] = 1;
  for (int x = 2; x <= n; ++x) {
    if (!vis[x]) {
      prime.emplace_back(x);
      f[x] = 1 - x;
    }
    for (int p : prime) {
      if (1LL * p * x > n) break;
      vis[x * p] = 1;
      f[x * p] = x % p ? (1 - p) * f[x] : f[x];
      if (x % p == 0) break;
    }
  }
  for (int x = 1; x <= n; ++x) {
    f[x] = 1LL * x * f[x] % M + M;
    f[x] = (f[x] + f[x - 1]) % M;
  }
  long long res = 0;
  for (int l = 1, r; l <= n; l = r + 1) {
    int nn = n / l, mm = m / l;
    r = std::min(n / nn, m / mm);
    int g_n = (1LL * nn * (nn + 1) / 2) % M;
    int g_m = (1LL * mm * (mm + 1) / 2) % M;
    res += 1LL * g_n * g_m % M * (f[r] - f[l - 1] + M) % M;
  }
  std::cout << (res % M) << '\n';
  return 0;
}

    The next example problem is special and requires transforming the divisor count function for products.

    LOJ 2185. [SDOI2015] Sum of Number of Divisors

    𝑇T test cases. For each test case, compute:

    𝑛∑𝑖=1𝑚∑𝑗=1𝜎0(𝑖𝑗).∑i=1n∑j=1mσ0(ij).

    Here, 𝜎0(𝑛) =∑𝑑∣𝑛1σ0(n)=∑d∣n1 represents the number of divisors of 𝑛n.

    Constraints: 1 ≤𝑛,𝑚,𝑇 ≤5 ×1041≤n,m,T≤5×104.

    Solution

    The difficulty of this problem is transforming 𝜎0(𝑖𝑗)σ0(ij) into an expression in terms of the greatest common divisor. Since 𝜎0σ0 is a multiplicative function, we first consider the case of prime powers. For a prime 𝑝p and non-negative exponents 𝑒1,𝑒2e1,e2, let 𝑖 =𝑝𝑒1, 𝑗 =𝑝𝑒2i=pe1, j=pe2, then

    𝜎0(𝑖𝑗)=1+𝑒1+𝑒2=∑𝑥∣𝑖∑𝑦∣𝑗[𝑥⟂𝑦].σ0(ij)=1+e1+e2=∑x∣i∑y∣j[x⟂y].

    For the general case, let 𝑖 =∏𝑝𝑖𝑝i=∏pip and 𝑗 =∏𝑝𝑗𝑝j=∏pjp, where 𝑖𝑝,𝑗𝑝ip,jp are respectively the powers of 𝑝p in the prime factorizations of 𝑖,𝑗i,j. Then

    𝜎0(𝑖𝑗)=∏𝑝𝜎0(𝑖𝑝𝑗𝑝)=∏𝑝∑𝑥𝑝∣𝑖𝑝∑𝑦𝑝∣𝑗𝑝[𝑥𝑝⟂𝑦𝑝].σ0(ij)=∏pσ0(ipjp)=∏p∑xp∣ip∑yp∣jp[xp⟂yp].

    Note that enumerating all divisors 𝑥𝑝xp of each prime power factor 𝑖𝑝ip of 𝑖i is equivalent to enumerating all divisors 𝑥x of 𝑖i and then decomposing into all prime power factors 𝑥𝑝xp; similarly for 𝑗j. Therefore, using the distributive law of multiplication, we have

    𝜎0(𝑖𝑗)=∑𝑥∣𝑖∑𝑦∣𝑗∏𝑝[𝑥𝑝⟂𝑦𝑝]=∑𝑥∣𝑖∑𝑦∣𝑗[𝑥⟂𝑦].σ0(ij)=∑x∣i∑y∣j∏p[xp⟂yp]=∑x∣i∑y∣j[x⟂y].

    The last step uses the conclusion: 𝑥 ⟂𝑦x⟂y if and only if for each prime factor 𝑝p, we have 𝑥𝑝 ⟂𝑦𝑝xp⟂yp.

    After obtaining this expression, we can apply the standard processing:

    𝜎0(𝑖𝑗)=∑𝑥∣𝑖∑𝑦∣𝑗[𝑥⟂𝑦]=∑𝑥∣𝑖∑𝑦∣𝑗∑𝑑𝜇(𝑑)[𝑑∣𝑥][𝑑∣𝑦]=∑𝑑𝜇(𝑑)(∑𝑥[𝑑∣𝑥∣𝑖])(∑𝑦[𝑑∣𝑦∣𝑗])=∑𝑑𝜇(𝑑)[𝑑∣𝑖][𝑑∣𝑗]𝜎0(𝑖𝑑)𝜎0(𝑗𝑑).σ0(ij)=∑x∣i∑y∣j[x⟂y]=∑x∣i∑y∣j∑dμ(d)[d∣x][d∣y]=∑dμ(d)(∑x[d∣x∣i])(∑y[d∣y∣j])=∑dμ(d)[d∣i][d∣j]σ0(id)σ0(jd).

    The meaning of the last step of derivation is: the function is nonzero only when 𝑑 ∣𝑖d∣i and 𝑑 ∣𝑗d∣j. At this time, enumerating 𝑥x satisfying 𝑑 ∣𝑥 ∣𝑖d∣x∣i is equivalent to enumerating divisors 𝑥𝑑xd of 𝑖𝑑id; similarly for 𝑦y and 𝑗j.

    Substitute this expression back into the original expression and swap the order of summation:

    𝑓(𝑛,𝑚)=𝑛∑𝑖=1𝑚∑𝑗=1𝜎0(𝑖𝑗)=𝑛∑𝑖=1𝑚∑𝑗=1∑𝑑𝜇(𝑑)[𝑑∣𝑖][𝑑∣𝑗]𝜎0(𝑖𝑑)𝜎0(𝑗𝑑)=∑𝑑𝜇(𝑑)(𝑛∑𝑖=1[𝑑∣𝑖]𝜎0(𝑖𝑑))(𝑚∑𝑗=1[𝑑∣𝑗]𝜎0(𝑗𝑑))=∑𝑑𝜇(𝑑)(⌊𝑛/𝑑⌋∑𝑖=1𝜎0(𝑖))(⌊𝑚/𝑑⌋∑𝑗=1𝜎0(𝑗)).f(n,m)=∑i=1n∑j=1mσ0(ij)=∑i=1n∑j=1m∑dμ(d)[d∣i][d∣j]σ0(id)σ0(jd)=∑dμ(d)(∑i=1n[d∣i]σ0(id))(∑j=1m[d∣j]σ0(jd))=∑dμ(d)(∑i=1⌊n/d⌋σ0(i))(∑j=1⌊m/d⌋σ0(j)).

    Let 𝐺(𝑛) =∑𝑛𝑖=1𝜎0(𝑖)G(n)=∑i=1nσ0(i), then

    𝑓(𝑛,𝑚)=∑𝑑𝜇(𝑑)𝐺(⌊𝑛𝑑⌋)𝐺(⌊𝑚𝑑⌋).f(n,m)=∑dμ(d)G(⌊nd⌋)G(⌊md⌋).

    This can be solved using number theoretic blocks. We only need to precompute the prefix sums of 𝜇(𝑛)μ(n) and 𝜎0(𝑛)σ0(n). The total time complexity is 𝑂(𝑁 +𝑇√𝑁)O(N+TN), where 𝑁N is the upper bound of 𝑛,𝑚n,m, and 𝑇T is the number of test cases.

    #include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
using namespace std;
constexpr long long N = 5e4 + 5;
long long n, m, T, pr[N], mu[N], d[N], t[N],
    cnt;  // t is the number of times the smallest prime factor of i appears
bool bp[N];

void prime_work(long long k) {
  bp[0] = bp[1] = true, mu[1] = 1, d[1] = 1;
  for (long long i = 2; i <= k; i++) {  // Linear sieve
    if (!bp[i]) pr[++cnt] = i, mu[i] = -1, d[i] = 2, t[i] = 1;
    for (long long j = 1; j <= cnt && i * pr[j] <= k; j++) {
      bp[i * pr[j]] = true;
      if (i % pr[j] == 0) {
        mu[i * pr[j]] = 0;
        d[i * pr[j]] = d[i] / (t[i] + 1) * (t[i] + 2);
        t[i * pr[j]] = t[i] + 1;
        break;
      } else {
        mu[i * pr[j]] = -mu[i];
        d[i * pr[j]] = d[i] << 1;
        t[i * pr[j]] = 1;
      }
    }
  }
  for (long long i = 2; i <= k; i++)
    mu[i] += mu[i - 1], d[i] += d[i - 1];  // Compute prefix sums
}

long long solve() {
  long long res = 0, mxi = min(n, m);
  for (long long i = 1, j; i <= mxi; i = j + 1) {  // Division block decomposition
    j = min(n / (n / i), m / (m / i));
    res += d[n / i] * d[m / i] * (mu[j] - mu[i - 1]);
  }
  return res;
}

int main() {
  cin.tie(nullptr)->sync_with_stdio(false);
  cin >> T;
  prime_work(50000);  // Preprocess
  while (T--) {
    cin >> n >> m;
    cout << solve() << '\n';
  }
  return 0;
}

    The final example problem demonstrates how to apply the multiplicative version of Möbius inversion.

    Luogu P5221 Product

    Compute:

    𝑛∏𝑖=1𝑛∏𝑗=1lcm⁡(𝑖,𝑗)gcd(𝑖,𝑗)(mod104857601).∏i=1n∏j=1nlcm⁡(i,j)gcd(i,j)(mod104857601).

    Constraints: 1 ≤𝑛 ≤1 ×1061≤n≤1×106.

    Solution One

    Ignore the modulus during derivation. Let

    𝑓(𝑛)=𝑛∏𝑖=1𝑛∏𝑗=1lcm⁡(𝑖,𝑗)gcd(𝑖,𝑗).f(n)=∏i=1n∏j=1nlcm⁡(i,j)gcd(i,j).

    Still converting the least common multiple to the greatest common divisor:

    𝑓(𝑛)=𝑛∏𝑖=1𝑛∏𝑗=1𝑖𝑗(gcd(𝑖,𝑗))2.f(n)=∏i=1n∏j=1nij(gcd(i,j))2.

    Note that the product of these factors is independent of each other and can be computed separately. Let

    𝑔(𝑛)=𝑛∏𝑖=1𝑛∏𝑗=1gcd(𝑖,𝑗).g(n)=∏i=1n∏j=1ngcd(i,j).

    Then the original expression equals:

    𝑓(𝑛)=(𝑛!)2𝑛𝑔(𝑛)2.f(n)=(n!)2ng(n)2.

    The key is to solve the computation problem of 𝑔(𝑛)g(n). The processing flow is similar to that described earlier, but we need to switch to the corresponding multiplicative version. First, enumerate and extract the common divisor:

    𝑔(𝑛)=∏𝑘𝑛∏𝑖=1𝑛∏𝑗=1𝑘↑[gcd(𝑖,𝑗)=𝑘]=∏𝑘⌊𝑛/𝑘⌋∏𝑖=1⌊𝑛/𝑘⌋∏𝑗=1𝑘↑[gcd(𝑖,𝑗)=1].g(n)=∏k∏i=1n∏j=1nk↑[gcd(i,j)=k]=∏k∏i=1⌊n/k⌋∏j=1⌊n/k⌋k↑[gcd(i,j)=1].

    Here, 𝑎 ↑𝑏 =𝑎𝑏a↑b=ab is Knuth's up-arrow notation. Then substitute [gcd(𝑖,𝑗) =1] =∑𝑑𝜇(𝑑)[𝑑 ∣𝑖][𝑑 ∣𝑗][gcd(i,j)=1]=∑dμ(d)[d∣i][d∣j], and convert the sum in the exponent to a product of powers:

    𝑔(𝑛)=∏𝑘∏𝑑⌊𝑛/𝑘⌋∏𝑖=1⌊𝑛/𝑘⌋∏𝑗=1𝑘↑(𝜇(𝑑)[𝑑∣𝑖][𝑑∣𝑗]).g(n)=∏k∏d∏i=1⌊n/k⌋∏j=1⌊n/k⌋k↑(μ(d)[d∣i][d∣j]).

    Further extract the factor (i.e., let 𝑖 =𝑑𝑖′i=di′, 𝑗 =𝑑𝑗′j=dj′), and apply the property of the floor function:

    𝑔(𝑛)=∏𝑘∏𝑑⌊𝑛/(𝑘𝑑)⌋∏𝑖=1⌊𝑛/(𝑘𝑑)⌋∏𝑗=1𝑘↑𝜇(𝑑).g(n)=∏k∏d∏i=1⌊n/(kd)⌋∏j=1⌊n/(kd)⌋k↑μ(d).

    Then separate the product regarding 𝑖,𝑗i,j, and we find the product does not contain 𝑖,𝑗i,j, so it is equivalent to raising the product to a power:

    𝑔(𝑛)=∏𝑘∏𝑑𝑘↑(𝜇(𝑑)⌊𝑛𝑘𝑑⌋2).g(n)=∏k∏dk↑(μ(d)⌊nkd⌋2).

    Since we enumerated common divisors earlier, for this expression we need to swap the order of multiplication again. Let ℓ =𝑘𝑑ℓ=kd:

    𝑔(𝑛)=∏ℓ∏𝑑∣ℓ(ℓ𝑑)↑(𝜇(𝑑)⌊𝑛ℓ⌋2)=∏ℓ⎛⎜ ⎜⎝∏𝑑∣ℓ(ℓ𝑑)↑𝜇(𝑑)⎞⎟ ⎟⎠↑⌊𝑛ℓ⌋2.g(n)=∏ℓ∏d∣ℓ(ℓd)↑(μ(d)⌊nℓ⌋2)=∏ℓ(∏d∣ℓ(ℓd)↑μ(d))↑⌊nℓ⌋2.

    Let

    𝐹(𝑛)=∏𝑑∣𝑛(𝑛𝑑)↑𝜇(𝑑).F(n)=∏d∣n(nd)↑μ(d).

    This is easily seen to be the Möbius inversion in product form for ˜𝐹(𝑛) =𝑛F~(n)=n. Even without knowing its expression, we can apply the Dirichlet difference method to preprocess in 𝑂(𝑛log⁡log⁡𝑛)O(nlog⁡log⁡n) time. Of course, since the form of ˜𝐹(𝑛)F~(n) is very simple, the expression for 𝐹(𝑛)F(n) can be directly obtained:

    𝐹(𝑛)={𝑝,𝑛=𝑝𝑒, 𝑝∈𝐏, 𝑒∈𝐍+,1,otherwise.F(n)={p,n=pe, p∈P, e∈N+,1,otherwise.

    The von Mangoldt function is its natural logarithm. After obtaining the values of 𝐹(𝑛)F(n), we can directly apply the product version of number theoretic blocks to compute 𝑔(𝑛)g(n) in 𝑂(√𝑛)O(n) time, and then obtain 𝑓(𝑛)f(n). The total time complexity is 𝑂(𝑛)O(n).

    It is worth noting that when computations involving products are involved, Euler's theorem is often needed, so the modulus used for the exponent part is different from the modulus given in the problem.

    Solution Two

    The difficulty of the product version derivation is that the handling of products and exponents is relatively unfamiliar. Therefore, for such problems, we can also take the logarithm first and then derive. For this problem, consider only the derivation of 𝑔(𝑛)g(n). After taking its logarithm:

    log⁡𝑔(𝑛)=𝑛∑𝑖=1𝑛∑𝑗=1log⁡gcd(𝑖,𝑗).log⁡g(n)=∑i=1n∑j=1nlog⁡gcd(i,j).

    For such expressions involving the greatest common divisor, directly applying the standard derivation process gives:

    log⁡𝑔(𝑛)=∑𝑘log⁡𝑘𝑛∑𝑖=1𝑛∑𝑗=1[gcd(𝑖,𝑗)=𝑘]=∑𝑘log⁡𝑘⌊𝑛/𝑘⌋∑𝑖=1⌊𝑛/𝑘⌋∑𝑗=1[gcd(𝑖,𝑗)=1]=∑𝑘log⁡𝑘∑𝑑𝜇(𝑑)(⌊𝑛/𝑘⌋∑𝑖=1[𝑖∣𝑑])(⌊𝑛/𝑘⌋∑𝑗=1[𝑗∣𝑑])=∑𝑘log⁡𝑘∑𝑑𝜇(𝑑)⌊𝑛𝑘𝑑⌋2=∑ℓ(∑𝑑𝜇(𝑑)log⁡ℓ𝑑)⌊𝑛ℓ⌋2=∑ℓΛ(ℓ)⌊𝑛ℓ⌋2.log⁡g(n)=∑klog⁡k∑i=1n∑j=1n[gcd(i,j)=k]=∑klog⁡k∑i=1⌊n/k⌋∑j=1⌊n/k⌋[gcd(i,j)=1]=∑klog⁡k∑dμ(d)(∑i=1⌊n/k⌋[i∣d])(∑j=1⌊n/k⌋[j∣d])=∑klog⁡k∑dμ(d)⌊nkd⌋2=∑ℓ(∑dμ(d)log⁡ℓd)⌊nℓ⌋2=∑ℓΛ(ℓ)⌊nℓ⌋2.

    Here, Λ(𝑛)Λ(n) is the von Mangoldt function. Taking the exponent of this derivation result gives the result in Solution One.

    #include <algorithm>
#include <iostream>
#include <vector>

int pow(int a, int b, int m) {
  int res = 1;
  for (int po = a; b; b >>= 1) {
    if (b & 1) res = 1LL * res * po % m;
    po = 1LL * po * po % m;
  }
  return res;
}

int main() {
  constexpr int M = 104857601;
  int n;
  std::cin >> n;
  // Get F(n), i.e., exp(Lambda(n)).
  std::vector<int> vis(n + 1), prime, pf(n + 1), rem(n + 1);
  prime.reserve(n);
  for (int x = 2; x <= n; ++x) {
    if (!vis[x]) {
      prime.emplace_back(x);
      pf[x] = x;
      rem[x] = 1;
    }
    for (int p : prime) {
      if (1LL * p * x > n) break;
      vis[x * p] = 1;
      pf[x * p] = p;
      rem[x * p] = x % p ? x : rem[x];
      if (x % p == 0) break;
    }
  }
  pf[1] = 1;
  for (int x = 2; x <= n; ++x) {
    pf[x] = rem[x] == 1 ? pf[x] : 1;
  }
  // Prefix products and their inverses.
  std::vector<int> pm(n + 1), ip(n + 1);
  pm[0] = 1;
  for (int x = 1; x <= n; ++x) {
    pm[x] = 1LL * pm[x - 1] * pf[x] % M;
  }
  int inv = pow(pm[n], M - 2, M);
  ip[0] = 1;
  for (int x = n; x >= 1; --x) {
    ip[x] = inv;
    inv = 1LL * inv * pf[x] % M;
  }
  // Calculate g(n).
  int res = 1;
  for (int l = 1, r; l <= n; l = r + 1) {
    r = n / (n / l);
    int a = 1LL * pm[r] * ip[l - 1] % M;
    int b = 1LL * (n / l) * (n / l) % (M - 1);
    res = 1LL * res * pow(a, b, M) % M;
  }
  // Take square and then inverse.
  res = pow(res, M - 3, M);
  // Get factorials.
  int fac = 1;
  for (int x = 1; x <= n; ++x) {
    fac = 1LL * fac * x % M;
  }
  // Final answer.
  res = 1LL * res * pow(fac, 2 * n, M) % M;
  std::cout << res << std::endl;
  return 0;
}
